**Nature of light.** Light was first regarded simply as radiant energy; at the beginning of the 20th century it was proved to be an **electromagnetic (EM) wave**, and later, through quantum theory, its **particle nature** was established, photons being the energy-carrier particles. An experiment using a countable number of photons settled the matter: light possesses a **dual nature**. In short, *light consists of energy-carrier photons guided by the rules of EM waves.* In vacuum these travel with speed \( c = 299792458\ \text{m s}^{-1} \), written for practical purposes as \( 3 \times 10^{8}\ \text{m s}^{-1} \).

**Which set of phenomena each picture explains:**

| Description used | Phenomena it explains |
|---|---|
| Wave optics (physical optics) | Interference, diffraction, polarization, Doppler effect |
| Particle (quantum) nature | Photoelectric effect, emission of spectral lines, Compton effect |

The wave picture treats light energy as EM waves; the particle picture is needed wherever light **interacts with matter**, which classical wave theory cannot describe.

**Phenomena explained by ray optics.** A ray is a particular direction of propagation of energy from a source of light. Ray optics (geometrical optics) satisfactorily explains **reflection, refraction, double refraction and total internal reflection**, and with them image formation by **mirrors, lenses and prisms**, dispersion by a prism, and everyday phenomena such as the mirage and the rainbow.

**The four fundamental laws / assumptions on which it is based:**

(i) Light travels in a **straight line** in a homogeneous and isotropic medium. *Homogeneous* means the properties of the medium are the same everywhere in it; *isotropic* means the properties are the same in all directions.

(ii) Two or more rays can **intersect at a point without affecting their paths** beyond that point.

(iii) **Laws of reflection:** (a) the reflected ray lies in the plane formed by the incident ray and the normal drawn at the point of incidence, the two rays being on either side of the normal; (b) the angles of incidence and reflection are equal.

(iv) **Laws of refraction** (at the boundary between two media): (a) the refracted ray lies in the plane formed by the incident ray and the normal at the point of incidence, the two rays being on either side of the normal; (b) Snell's law, \( n_{1}\sin\theta_{1} = n_{2}\sin\theta_{2} \).

All four can in fact be derived from a single principle — **Fermat's principle**, that a ray of light travelling from one point to another by one or more reflections or refractions always chooses the path of least (strictly, extreme) time.

**Focal power.** The converging or diverging ability of a lens or of a mirror is defined as its **focal power**, measured as \( P = \dfrac{1}{f} \). In SI units it is measured in **dioptre (D)**, so \( 1\ \text{dioptre} = 1\ \text{m}^{-1} \) — which means \( f \) must be substituted in metres.

**Why the reciprocal of \( f \) is a sensible measure.** The *smaller* the focal length, the *more strongly* the device bends a parallel incident beam — a short-focus lens brings the beam to a focus in a short distance, i.e. it converges more powerfully. Power must therefore *increase* as \( f \) *decreases*, and the simplest quantity with that behaviour is \( 1/f \).

The choice has two further conveniences: the sign is carried automatically (a converging lens or a concave mirror of positive/negative \( f \) keeps its own sign of \( P \)), and for **thin lenses in contact** the powers simply **add**, since \( \dfrac{1}{f} = \dfrac{1}{f_{1}} + \dfrac{1}{f_{2}} \) becomes \( P = P_{1} + P_{2} \).

**Convex mirror.** For *any* position of a real object a convex mirror always forms a virtual, erect and **diminished** image \( (m < 1) \). It can never magnify.

**Concave mirror.** Here the result depends on where the object is placed, as summarised in Table 9.2 of the chapter:

| Position of object | Position of image | Real / Virtual | \( m \) |
|---|---|---|---|
| \( u = \infty \) | \( v = f \) | R | \( m = 0 \) |
| \( u > 2f \) | \( 2f > v > f \) | R | \( m < 1 \) |
| \( u = 2f \) | \( v = 2f \) | R | \( m = 1 \) |
| \( 2f > u > f \) | \( v > 2f \) | R | \( m > 1 \) |
| \( u = f \) | \( v = \infty \) | R | \( m = \infty \) |
| \( u < f \) | \( |v| > |u| \) | V | \( m > 1 \) |

**(i) Diminished image** — a convex mirror for every object position, and a concave mirror when the object is **beyond the centre of curvature** \( (u > 2f) \), including an object at infinity.

**(ii) Magnified image** — only a concave mirror, and only when the object lies **within the centre of curvature**: between \( C \) and \( F \) \( (2f > u > f) \), giving a real inverted magnified image, or **within the focus** \( (u < f) \), giving a virtual erect magnified image.

The relations \( f = \dfrac{R}{2} \) and \( \dfrac{1}{f} = \dfrac{1}{v} + \dfrac{1}{u} \) are not exact; they are derived under restrictions, and an image is appreciably clear only while those restrictions hold. They are:

(i) **Objects and images must be situated close to the principal axis** — an object far off the axis gives an image spoilt by coma, astigmatism, curvature and distortion.

(ii) **Rays diverging from the object must be confined to a cone of very small angle**, i.e. the mirror must be of **small aperture** (its diameter at least ten times smaller than the values of \( u \), \( v \) and \( f \)). A wide aperture admits marginal rays, which focus nearer the pole than paraxial rays and produce spherical aberration — an unsharp image with unclear boundaries.

(iii) **A parallel incident beam must be paraxial**, i.e. parallel to and close to the principal axis.

If these are not satisfied the image is not a point but a circle; at one particular screen position that circle is smallest and is called the **circle of least confusion**.

**Spherical aberration for spherical mirrors.** The relation \( f = \dfrac{R}{2} \), which gives a single point focus, holds only for a small-aperture spherical mirror and for paraxial rays. In reality, as the incident rays are taken farther from the principal axis, the focus **gradually shifts towards the pole**. This defect, arising from the spherical shape of the reflecting surface itself, is called **spherical aberration**. It produces an unsharp (fuzzy) image with unclear boundaries: no screen position gives a point image, the image is always a circle, and the distance between the marginal focus \( F_{M} \) and the paraxial focus \( F_{P} \) is the **longitudinal spherical aberration**. The screen position at which that circle is smallest gives the **circle of least confusion**, whose radius is the transverse spherical aberration.

**How it is minimized.** By **reducing the aperture** of the mirror — restricting the beam to paraxial rays, e.g. by stopping down the mirror — so that all the reflected rays cross close to the same point.

**Can it be eliminated?** Yes, but not by a spherical mirror. Using a **parabolic mirror** removes it completely. A parabola is drawn so that every point on it is equidistant from a straight line (the directrix) and a point (the focus); consequently the optical paths of all rays of a beam parallel to the axis are equal right up to the focus, so the whole beam — marginal rays included — converges to a **single** point. This is why the mirrors of a search light, a torch, a car headlight and a telescope are made parabolic and not spherical.

**Absolute refractive index.** The absolute refractive index of a medium is the **ratio of the speed of light in vacuum to that in the given medium**:
\( n = \dfrac{c}{v} \)
Being the ratio of two like quantities it is **unitless and dimensionless**. For every material medium (air included) \( n > 1 \), because light travels fastest in vacuum. A medium of greater \( n \) is called **optically denser** — and optically denser need not mean physically denser: many oils are optically denser than water although water is physically denser than them.
*Illustration:* for glass \( n = 1.5 \), so light travels through glass at \( \dfrac{3 \times 10^{8}}{1.5} = 2 \times 10^{8}\ \text{m/s} \).

**Relative refractive index.** The refractive index of medium 2 **with respect to** medium 1 is the ratio of the speed \( v_{1} \) in medium 1 to the speed \( v_{2} \) in medium 2:
\( {}^{1}n_{2} = \dfrac{n_{2}}{n_{1}} = \dfrac{v_{1}}{v_{2}} \)
The notation says that \( n_{2} \) (medium 2) is being discussed *in the context of* medium 1, light travelling from 1 to 2.
*Illustration:* for light passing from water \( (n_{1} = 4/3) \) into glass \( (n_{2} = 3/2) \), \( {}^{1}n_{2} = \dfrac{3/2}{4/3} = \dfrac{9}{8} \), so glass is optically denser than water and the ray bends towards the normal.

**Mirage.** On a hot, clear, sunny day a pond of water appears to lie ahead along a level road; on reaching the spot there is only dry road, and the pond appears ahead again. This illusion is a **mirage**, and it is an illustration of refraction through a medium whose refractive index varies continuously.

**Explanation.** The air in contact with the hot road is the **hottest and therefore optically rarest**, and as one goes up the air gets gradually cooler and optically denser — the refractive index of air **increases with height**. A ray of light coming downwards from the top of a distant object (a tree, say) therefore passes continuously from denser to rarer air and bends **away from the normal** at every level, becoming more and more horizontal until it almost grazes the road. It then bends upwards and, travelling into denser air, continues to bend upwards. Reaching the observer from below, it appears to come from beneath the object, giving the illusion of a reflection in an imaginary water surface.

**A caution.** The upward bending at the road is **not** total internal reflection. As the chapter points out, the relative refractive index of the successive air layers is only just less than 1, so the critical angle is approaching \( 90^\circ \) and total internal reflection is never possible here. The likely reasons are that at grazing incidence the reflection coefficient is very large, and that the unsteady, non-uniformly moving air just above the hot road bends the ray upwards — once it has begun to bend upwards it continues to do so.

**Conditions for total internal reflection (TIR).** Two conditions must hold together:
(i) light must travel from an **optically denser medium into an optically rarer** medium, and
(ii) the angle of incidence in the denser medium must be **greater than the critical angle** \( i_{c} \) for that pair of media.

In general there is always partial reflection and partial refraction at an interface. During TIR there is **total reflection and no refraction** — hence the name.

**Critical angle.** The critical angle for a pair of refracting media is that **angle of incidence in the denser medium for which the angle of refraction in the rarer medium is \( 90^\circ \)**. For angles of incidence greater than \( i_{c} \) the refracted ray would need an angle beyond \( 90^\circ \), which is impossible, so the ray does not enter the rarer medium at all and is reflected wholly back into the denser one.

**Expression.** Let \( \mu \) be the refractive index of the denser medium relative to the rarer. Applying Snell's law at \( i = i_{c} \), \( r = 90^\circ \):
\( \mu \sin(i_{c}) = (1)\sin 90^\circ \)
\( \therefore \sin(i_{c}) = \dfrac{1}{\mu} \quad \text{i.e.} \quad i_{c} = \sin^{-1}\left( \dfrac{1}{\mu} \right) \)
For commonly used glass, \( \mu = 1.5 \Rightarrow i_{c} = 41^\circ 49' \approx 42^\circ \); for water, \( \mu = \dfrac{4}{3} \Rightarrow i_{c} = 48^\circ 35' \) (both with respect to air).

**Example.** In an **optical fibre** the transparent core is optically denser than the surrounding cladding, and a signal entering the core strikes the core–cladding boundary at an angle greater than the critical angle. It is therefore totally internally reflected again and again, and emerges after several kilometres with extremely low loss.

**Construction.** An optical fibre consists of an extremely thin (slightly thicker than a human hair), transparent, flexible **core**, surrounded by an optically **rarer** (smaller refractive index) flexible cover called the **cladding**. This is coated by a **buffer** and a **jacket** for protection. The entire thickness of one fibre is less than half a millimetre, and a number of such fibres may be packed together in an outer cover.

**Working.** Because the core is optically denser than the cladding, an optical signal launched into the core meets the core–cladding boundary at an angle greater than the critical angle and suffers **repeated total internal reflection**. Since total internal reflection involves no refraction, essentially no energy leaks out at each bounce, and the signal emerges after several kilometres travelling at the highest possible speed in that material (about \( 2{,}00{,}000\ \text{km/s} \) for glass).

**Advantages over electronic communication:**

(a) **Broad bandwidth** — for TV signals a single fibre can carry over 90000 independent channels.
(b) **Immune to EM interference** — being electrically non-conductive it cannot pick up nearby EM signals.
(c) **Low attenuation loss** — below 0.2 dB/km, so one long cable serves several kilometres.
(d) **Electrical insulator** — no problem with ground loops of metal wires, or with lightning.
(e) **Theft prevention** — it uses no copper or other expensive material.
(f) **Security of information** — internal damage (and hence tapping) is most unlikely.

Its one drawback is the relatively high cost of the initial set-up.

**Why prism binoculars are preferred.** In binoculars using only two straight cylinders, the distance between the two objectives cannot be greater than the distance between the two eyes. That limits the separation of the objectives and hence the **field of view** (and the stereoscopic effect). Prism binoculars overcome this limitation: by folding the light path, the objectives can be set **wider apart than the eyes**, giving a **wider input range** and so a larger field of view, while the instrument itself stays short.

**Working.** The folding is done with **two right-angled isosceles glass prisms** in each barrel, used for **total internal reflection**. Light entering the widely-spaced objective strikes the hypotenuse face of the first prism at \( 45^\circ \), which is greater than the critical angle for glass \( (i_{c} \approx 42^\circ) \); it is therefore totally internally reflected through \( 90^\circ \). The second prism, set at right angles to the first, turns it through \( 90^\circ \) once more, bringing the beam inward to the eyepiece. The two reflections together also **re-invert** the image, so the final view is erect.

Total internal reflection is used rather than metal mirrors because it is loss-free — a mirror always absorbs some light at each reflection, whereas TIR reflects the beam completely.

**Refraction at a single spherical surface.** Let a spherical surface of radius of curvature \( R \) with pole \( P \) and centre of curvature \( C \) separate two media of refractive indices \( n_{1} \) (the medium of the real object) and \( n_{2} \) (the other medium). Let \( O \) be a point object on the principal axis at distance \( u \), and let the refracted rays meet the axis at \( I \), at distance \( v \).

Consider the axial ray \( OP \), which travels undeviated, and a paraxial ray \( OA \) striking the surface at \( A \). Since \( n_{1} < n_{2} \) the ray \( OA \) deviates towards the normal \( CA \) and cuts the axis at \( I \).

By Snell's law at \( A \):
\( n_{1}\sin(i) = n_{2}\sin(r) \)

Let \( \alpha, \beta, \gamma \) be the angles subtended at the axis by the incident ray, the normal and the refracted ray. From the exterior-angle property of a triangle,
\( i = \alpha + \beta \quad \text{and} \quad r = \beta - \gamma \)

**Assumptions:** the rays are **paraxial** and the aperture is **small**, so all these angles are small. Hence \( \sin(i) \cong i \), \( \sin(r) \cong r \), and the arc \( AP \) may be treated as a straight line perpendicular to the axis, giving
\( \alpha \cong \dfrac{\text{arc }AP}{PO} = \dfrac{\text{arc }AP}{-u} \), \( \beta = \dfrac{\text{arc }AP}{PC} = \dfrac{\text{arc }AP}{R} \), \( \gamma \cong \dfrac{\text{arc }AP}{PI} = \dfrac{\text{arc }AP}{v} \)

Snell's law now reads \( n_{1}i = n_{2}r \), i.e.
\( n_{1}(\alpha + \beta) = n_{2}(\beta - \gamma) \)
\( \therefore (n_{2} - n_{1})\beta = n_{2}\gamma + n_{1}\alpha \)

Substituting for \( \alpha, \beta, \gamma \) and cancelling \( \text{arc }AP \):
\( \dfrac{n_{2} - n_{1}}{R} = \dfrac{n_{2}}{v} - \dfrac{n_{1}}{u} \)

All the symbolic values were substituted as per the **Cartesian sign convention**, so this expression applies to any surface separating any two media and to a real or a virtual image, provided values are substituted with their proper signs. The only restriction is that \( n_{1} \) must be the refractive index of the medium of the **real object** and \( n_{2} \) that of the *other* medium — not necessarily the medium of the image.

**Lens makers' equation.** Consider a thin lens of refractive index \( n \) with respect to the outside medium, with radii of curvature \( R_{1} \) and \( R_{2} \). Being thin, both surfaces share the common pole \( P \). Let \( O \) be a point object on the axis at distance \( u \), the first surface \( R_{1} \) facing the object.

**First refraction.** In \( \dfrac{n_{2} - n_{1}}{R} = \dfrac{n_{2}}{v} - \dfrac{n_{1}}{u} \), put \( n_{1} = 1 \), \( n_{2} = n \), \( R = R_{1} \), \( v = v_{1} \) (the intermediate image \( I_{1} \)):
\( \dfrac{n - 1}{R_{1}} = \dfrac{n}{v_{1}} - \dfrac{1}{u} \) ... (1)

**Second refraction.** \( I_{1} \) acts as a **virtual object** for the second surface, so \( u = v_{1} \); here the incident rays are inside the lens, so \( n_{1} = n \), \( n_{2} = 1 \), \( R = R_{2} \), and \( v \) is the final image distance:
\( \dfrac{1 - n}{R_{2}} = \dfrac{1}{v} - \dfrac{n}{v_{1}} \) ... (2)

**Adding (1) and (2)**, the \( v_{1} \) terms cancel:
\( (n - 1)\left( \dfrac{1}{R_{1}} - \dfrac{1}{R_{2}} \right) = \dfrac{1}{v} - \dfrac{1}{u} \)

For \( u = \infty \), \( v = f \), giving
\( \dfrac{1}{f} = (n - 1)\left( \dfrac{1}{R_{1}} - \dfrac{1}{R_{2}} \right) \)

**Why it is so called.** For preparing spectacles and other lenses it is necessary to *grind the glass (or acrylic) to the required radii of curvature*. This equation is what tells the maker which radii will give the desired focal length for the chosen material — it is used by the **maker of the lens**, hence the name.

**When \( |f| = |R| \) numerically.** Take a thin, symmetric double lens, so that \( |R_{1}| = |R_{2}| = R \).
- Double convex: \( R_{1} = +R \), \( R_{2} = -R \), so \( \dfrac{1}{f} = (n-1)\dfrac{2}{R} \). If \( n = 1.5 \), then \( f = R \).
- Double concave: \( R_{1} = -R \), \( R_{2} = +R \), so \( \dfrac{1}{f} = \dfrac{-2(n-1)}{R} \). If \( n = 1.5 \), then \( f = -R \).

So focal length and radius of curvature are numerically equal for a **thin symmetric double lens made of material of refractive index 1.5** (the popular variety of glass).

The refractive index of a material depends on the frequency of the light and **increases with frequency**. Hence for an obliquely incident polychromatic beam the angle of refraction is different for each colour, and the colours **separate out (disperse)** as they travel along different directions. There are two types.

**(1) Angular dispersion.** When a polychromatic beam is obliquely incident on a refracting surface, the emergent rays of different colours travel along **different directions**, i.e. they are separated in angle. The angle between the extreme colours is the angular dispersion, \( \delta_{VR} = \delta_{V} - \delta_{R} \). It occurs because each colour has its own refractive index and therefore its own angle of refraction. This is what a prism produces, and it is why a prism gives a spectrum.

**(2) Lateral dispersion.** If the polychromatic beam is obliquely incident on a **plane parallel transparent slab**, the emergent rays of all the colours come out **parallel to one another and parallel to the original direction** — the angular separation acquired at the first surface is exactly undone at the second. What survives is a small sideways displacement: each colour is laterally shifted by a different amount, and the perpendicular distance between the extreme emergent rays, \( L_{VR} = L_{V} - L_{R} \), is the lateral dispersion. It occurs because the colours travel along slightly different paths *inside* the slab. For it to be detectable at all, the parallel surfaces must be separated by a very large distance and the angle of incidence must be large — for an ordinary slab it is far too small to detect.

**Definition.** If a polychromatic beam is incident upon a prism, the emergent beam consists of all the component colours angularly separated. **Angular dispersion** is the **angle between the emergent rays of any two component colours**, measured as the difference of their angles of deviation:
\( \delta_{21} = \delta_{2} - \delta_{1} \)
Normally it is quoted for the **extreme colours** of white light, violet and red:
\( \delta_{VR} = \delta_{V} - \delta_{R} \)

**Expression for a thin prism.** A prism of refracting angle \( A < 10^\circ \) is a thin prism. For such a prism (and for small \( i \), so that all the angles are small) \( \sin\theta \cong \theta \), so
\( n = \dfrac{\sin i}{\sin r_{1}} \cong \dfrac{i}{r_{1}} \) and \( n = \dfrac{\sin e}{\sin r_{2}} \cong \dfrac{e}{r_{2}} \)
\( \therefore i \cong n r_{1} \) and \( e \cong n r_{2} \)
Using these in \( i + e = A + \delta \):
\( i + e = n r_{1} + n r_{2} = n(r_{1} + r_{2}) = nA = A + \delta \)
\( \therefore \boxed{\ \delta = A(n - 1)\ } \)
Since \( A \) and \( n \) are constant for a given prism, the deviation of a thin prism is **independent of the angle of incidence**.

**Relation with the refractive indices.** Applying \( \delta = A(n-1) \) to each colour,
\( \delta_{21} = \delta_{2} - \delta_{1} = A(n_{2} - 1) - A(n_{1} - 1) = A(n_{2} - n_{1}) \)
and for the extreme colours,
\( \delta_{VR} = \delta_{V} - \delta_{R} = A(n_{V} - 1) - A(n_{R} - 1) = A(n_{V} - n_{R}) \)

Thus the angular dispersion is **directly proportional both to the refracting angle of the prism and to the difference of the refractive indices** for the two colours.

**Meaning.** Two prisms of the same refracting angle, made of different materials, spread white light through different angles. The ability of an optical material to disperse the constituent colours is its **dispersive power**. It is measured for any two colours as the **ratio of the angular dispersion to the mean deviation** for those two colours.

**Definition and expression in terms of angles of deviation.** For the extreme colours of white light,
\( \omega = \dfrac{\left[ \delta_{V} - \delta_{R} \right]}{\left[ \dfrac{\delta_{V} + \delta_{R}}{2} \right]} \cong \dfrac{\delta_{V} - \delta_{R}}{\delta_{Y}} \)
Here yellow is practically chosen as the mean colour for violet and red, so that the mean deviation \( \dfrac{\delta_{V} + \delta_{R}}{2} \cong \delta_{Y} \). (If you look at a rainbow widthwise, yellow appears centrally located, which is the reason for that choice.)

**Expression in terms of refractive indices.** Using \( \delta = A(n-1) \) for a thin prism,
\( \omega = \dfrac{A(n_{V} - n_{R})}{A(n_{Y} - 1)} = \dfrac{n_{V} - n_{R}}{n_{Y} - 1} \)

**Consequences.** \( A \) cancels, so \( \omega \) is a property of the **material only** — it does not depend on the dimensions or the refracting angle of the prism. Being the ratio of two like quantities it is **unitless and dimensionless**. For commonly used glasses it is around **0.03**, while for a dense flint glass it can be more than three times as large. Although \( \omega \) is obtained here with the thin-prism formula, the expression is valid for equilateral and right-angled prisms as well.

**(i) Conditions under which a rainbow can be seen.** A light shower with relatively large raindrops, morning or evening time, and enough sunlight. It is seen **during rains and on the side opposite to the Sun**, and only in the mornings and evenings — not throughout the day, because at midday the Sun is too high for the deviated rays to reach an observer on the ground.

**Optical phenomena involved.** Sunlight incident on a water drop deviates and disperses during refraction, is reflected **internally (NOT total internally)** once for a primary rainbow or twice for a secondary rainbow, and finally refracts again into air. At all stages there is angular dispersion, which leads to a clear separation of the colours.

**(ii) Primary rainbow.** A white ray \( AB \) from the Sun strikes the **upper** portion of a spherical drop at an incident angle \( i \). On entering the water it deviates and disperses; the extreme colours violet and red separate. These refracted rays \( BV \) and \( BR \) strike the opposite inner surface and suffer **one** internal (not total internal) reflection. The reflected rays finally emerge from \( V' \) and \( R' \) and reach an observer on the ground, appearing to come from the side opposite the Sun. The minimum-deviation rays of red and violet are inclined to the ground at \( \theta_{R} = 42.8^\circ \cong 43^\circ \) and \( \theta_{V} = 40.8^\circ \cong 41^\circ \). It is therefore visible in the angular range **about \( 41^\circ \) to \( 43^\circ \)** with the horizontal, and in the bow the **red is outer and violet inner**.

**(iii) Secondary rainbow.** Here the white ray strikes the **lower** portion of the drop; the refracted rays undergo **two** internal reflections before emerging from \( V' \) and \( R' \). The minimum-deviation rays are inclined to the ground at \( \theta_{R} \cong 51^\circ \) and \( \theta_{V} \cong 53^\circ \), so it is visible in the range **about \( 51^\circ \) to \( 53^\circ \)**. Because of the extra reflection the order is reversed: the **violet is outer and red is inner**, and it is fainter, since some light is lost at each internal reflection.

**(iv) Both together.** Yes. The two occupy **different, non-overlapping angular ranges** \( (41^\circ - 43^\circ \) and \( 51^\circ - 53^\circ) \), so a few lucky observers see two rainbows simultaneously, one concentric above the other, with the darker band between them. The conditions are the same as for a rainbow at all, but with enough sunlight and large enough drops for the doubly-reflected (and therefore much weaker) secondary bow to remain visible. Seen from a high altitude, e.g. an aeroplane, each can even appear as a **complete circle**.

**(i) Chromatic aberration for spherical lenses.** In the case of mirrors there is no dispersion, because no refractive index is involved. A lens, however, is made of a transparent material whose refractive index is **different for different colours**, so angular dispersion is present: a convex lens can be approximated to two thin prisms joined base to base, and a concave lens to two prisms joined vertex to vertex. If the lens is thick, a polychromatic beam such as white light is therefore brought to **notably different foci for each colour**, **violet being focused closest to the pole** since it has the maximum deviation. This defect is called **chromatic aberration**; longitudinal chromatic aberration, transverse chromatic aberration and the circle of least confusion are defined exactly as for spherical aberration.

**How to minimize or eliminate it.** Eliminating it *simultaneously for all colours is impossible*. We try to eliminate it for the **extreme colours**, which reduces it for the others. The convenient methods are to use either a **convex and a concave lens in contact**, or **two thin convex lenses with proper separation**. Such a combination is called an **achromatic combination**.

**(ii) Achromatism and its condition.** *Achromatism* is the condition in which the resultant focal length of a lens combination is the **same for both extreme colours**, so that the combination forms a single image free of colour fringes.

For two thin lenses in contact, \( \dfrac{1}{f} = \dfrac{1}{f_{1}} + \dfrac{1}{f_{2}} \), used separately for each colour. Achromatism requires
\( f_{V} = f_{R} \quad \text{i.e.} \quad \dfrac{1}{f_{V}} = \dfrac{1}{f_{R}} \)
\( \therefore \dfrac{1}{f_{1V}} + \dfrac{1}{f_{2V}} = \dfrac{1}{f_{1R}} + \dfrac{1}{f_{2R}} \)
Writing \( K_{1} = \left( \dfrac{1}{R_{1}} - \dfrac{1}{R_{2}} \right)_{1} \) and \( K_{2} = \left( \dfrac{1}{R_{1}} - \dfrac{1}{R_{2}} \right)_{2} \) and using the lens makers' equation for each colour,
\( (n_{1V} - 1)K_{1} + (n_{2V} - 1)K_{2} = (n_{1R} - 1)K_{1} + (n_{2R} - 1)K_{2} \)
\( \therefore \dfrac{K_{1}}{K_{2}} = \dfrac{n_{2V} - n_{2R}}{n_{1V} - n_{1R}} \) ... (1)

For the mean colour yellow, \( \dfrac{1}{f_{1Y}} = (n_{1Y} - 1)K_{1} \) and \( \dfrac{1}{f_{2Y}} = (n_{2Y} - 1)K_{2} \), so
\( \dfrac{K_{1}}{K_{2}} = \left( \dfrac{n_{2Y} - 1}{n_{1Y} - 1} \right)\left( \dfrac{f_{2Y}}{f_{1Y}} \right) \) ... (2)

Equating (1) and (2) and rearranging,
\( \dfrac{f_{2Y}}{f_{1Y}} = -\left( \dfrac{n_{2V} - n_{2R}}{n_{2Y} - 1} \right) \div \left( \dfrac{n_{1V} - n_{1R}}{n_{1Y} - 1} \right) = -\dfrac{\omega_{2}}{\omega_{1}} \)

This is the **condition for an achromatic combination of two lenses in contact**.

**Conditions for it to be converging.** Dispersive power \( \omega \) is always positive, so the ratio \( \dfrac{f_{2Y}}{f_{1Y}} \) is negative: **one lens must be convex and the other concave**. If the second lens is concave, \( f_{2Y} \) is negative and \( \dfrac{1}{f_{Y}} = \dfrac{1}{f_{1Y}} - \dfrac{1}{f_{2Y}} \); for the combination to converge, \( f_{Y} \) must be positive, which requires
\( f_{1Y} < f_{2Y} \quad \text{and} \quad \omega_{1} < \omega_{2} \)
Thus the **convergent (convex) lens must have the smaller focal length and the smaller dispersive power**. Given a choice between flint glass \( (n = 1.655) \) and crown glass \( (n = 1.517) \), the convex lens must be of **crown** glass and the divergent concave lens of **flint** glass.

**Spherical aberration for spherical lenses.** While deriving the lens relations we assume most of the rays to be **paraxial**, by using lenses of small aperture. In reality objects are of finite size and, for telescopes and the like, we need lenses of large aperture — a few metres across. The beam is then no longer paraxial and quite often not even parallel. Consequently the marginal rays and the paraxial rays are brought to **different foci** \( (F_{m} \text{ and } F_{P}) \), exactly as for a spherical mirror. This is **spherical aberration**, it occurs for a monochromatic beam (no colour is involved), and it makes the image unsharp with unclear boundaries — longitudinal and transverse spherical aberration and the circle of least confusion being defined as before.

**Different ways to reduce or eliminate it:**

(i) The **cheapest** method is to use a **planoconvex or planoconcave** lens with its **curved side facing the incident rays** (the real object). Reversing the lens increases the aberration appreciably.

(ii) For a given refractive index a **certain ratio of the radii of curvature** almost eliminates it. For \( n = 1.5 \) the ratio is \( \dfrac{R_{1}}{R_{2}} = \dfrac{1}{6} \), and for \( n = 2 \) it is \( \dfrac{1}{5} \).

(iii) Using **two thin converging lenses separated by a distance equal to the difference between their focal lengths**, with the lens of larger focal length facing the incident rays, considerably reduces spherical aberration.

(iv) Spherical aberration of a convex lens is **positive** (for a real image) while that of a concave lens is **negative**. A suitable combination of the two — preferably a double convex lens of smaller focal length with a planoconcave lens of greater focal length — can therefore **completely eliminate** it.

**Why an angular measure is needed.** Whether an object appears big does not depend on its own size but on the **visual angle** it subtends at the eye: huge mountains far off look smaller than a small tree close by. To make something appear bigger we must increase that visual angle. But the eye cannot focus an object nearer than the **least distance of distinct vision** \( D \) (about 25 cm for a normal eye), and distant objects such as stars cannot be brought closer at all. Optical instruments exist to increase the visual angle, and that increase is what must be measured.

**Definition.** The **magnifying power** (angular magnification) of an optical instrument is the **ratio of the visual angle made by the image formed by that instrument \( (\beta) \) to the visual angle subtended by the object when kept at the least distance of distinct vision \( (\alpha) \)**:
\( M = \dfrac{\beta}{\alpha} \)
In the case of a **telescope**, \( \alpha \) is taken as the angle subtended by the object **from its own position**, since it is not possible to bring it closer.

**How it differs from linear (lateral) magnification.**

| | Linear / lateral magnification \( m \) | Magnifying power \( M \) |
|---|---|---|
| Definition | \( m = \dfrac{\text{image size}}{\text{object size}} = \dfrac{v}{u} \) | \( M = \dfrac{\beta}{\alpha} \) |
| Compares | Two **lengths**, measured perpendicular to the principal axis | Two **angles** subtended at the eye |
| Depends on | Only where the object and image are | Also on where the **eye** is, and on \( D \) |

The two are genuinely different quantities, and the chapter's own worked case shows it: for a simple microscope used with \( M_{min} = \dfrac{D}{f} = 5 \), the image is at infinity so \( m = \dfrac{v}{u} = \infty \) — the image size is infinitely large — yet the object appears only 5 times bigger. Only when the image happens to lie at \( D \) do the two numbers coincide.

**Simple microscope.** A convex lens used as a reading glass is a simple microscope. Fig. 9.26 (a) shows the visual angle \( \alpha \) made by an object kept at the least distance of distinct vision \( D \); without an instrument this is the greatest possible visual angle. In Fig. 9.26 (b) the object is placed **within the focus** of a convex lens, which forms an erect, virtual, magnified image. The visual angle \( \beta \) of the object and of its image are the same, but the viewer now looks at an image that is **not closer than \( D \)**, while the object itself is at a distance smaller than \( D \). Hence \( \beta > \alpha \) and the object appears bigger.

**Expression.** By definition \( M = \dfrac{\beta}{\alpha} \). For small angles,
\( M = \dfrac{\beta}{\alpha} \cong \dfrac{\tan\beta}{\tan\alpha} = \dfrac{\left( \dfrac{BA}{PA} \right)}{\left( \dfrac{BA}{D} \right)} = \dfrac{D}{u} \) (numerically)

**Limiting cases.**

**(i) Maximum magnifying power** — the image should be as near as possible, i.e. at \( D \). For a thin lens \( \dfrac{1}{f} = \dfrac{1}{v} - \dfrac{1}{u} \); here \( v = v_{min} = -D \) and \( u = -u \), so
\( \dfrac{1}{f} = \dfrac{1}{-D} - \dfrac{1}{-u} \quad \therefore \dfrac{D}{f} = \dfrac{D}{-D} + \dfrac{D}{u} \)
\( \therefore M_{max} = \dfrac{D}{u} = 1 + \dfrac{D}{f} \)

**(ii) Minimum magnifying power** — for \( v = \infty \), i.e. \( u = f \) numerically:
\( M_{min} = \dfrac{D}{u} = \dfrac{D}{f} \)

Thus the angular magnification by a lens of focal length \( f \) lies **between \( \dfrac{D}{f} \) and \( 1 + \dfrac{D}{f} \) only** — a range of exactly 1, whatever \( f \) may be. For a normal eye \( D = 25\ \text{cm} \), so a lens of \( f = 5\ \text{cm} \) gives \( M_{min} = 5 \) and \( M_{max} = 6 \): the image appears only 5 to 6 times bigger.

**Construction.** A compound microscope uses two convex lenses of suitable focal lengths fitted into a cylindrical tube whose length can be adjusted. The smaller lens (about 4 mm to 6 mm aperture) facing the object is the **objective**; the other, at which the observer jams the eye, is a little larger and is called the **eye lens**.

**Image formation.** A tiny object \( AB \) is placed between \( f \) and \( 2f \) of the objective, which produces a real, inverted, magnified image \( A'B' \). The eye lens is positioned so that \( A'B' \) falls **within its focus**; the eye lens therefore behaves as a simple microscope and produces the virtual, magnified final image \( A''B'' \), which is inverted with respect to the original object.

**Magnifying power.** From its position the final image \( A''B'' \) makes a visual angle \( \beta \) at the eye, and the object from distance \( D \) makes \( \alpha \):
\( \tan\beta = \dfrac{A''B''}{v_{e}} = \dfrac{A'B'}{u_{e}} \qquad \tan\alpha = \dfrac{AB}{D} \)
\( \therefore M = \dfrac{\beta}{\alpha} \cong \dfrac{\tan\beta}{\tan\alpha} = \left( \dfrac{A'B'}{u_{e}} \right) \times \left( \dfrac{D}{AB} \right) = \left( \dfrac{A'B'}{AB} \right) \times \left( \dfrac{D}{u_{e}} \right) \)
\( \therefore \boxed{\ M = m_{o} \times M_{e}\ } \)
where \( \left( \dfrac{A'B'}{AB} \right) = m_{o} = \dfrac{v_{o}}{u_{o}} \) is the **linear (lateral) magnification of the objective** and \( \left( \dfrac{D}{u_{e}} \right) = M_{e} \) is the **angular magnification of the eye lens**.

Since the eye lens acts as a simple microscope, \( M_{e} = \dfrac{D}{f_{e}} \) for the final image at infinity and \( M_{e} = 1 + \dfrac{D}{f_{e}} \) for the final image at \( D \); these give the minimum and maximum magnifying powers of the microscope.

**Length of the microscope.** It is simply the distance between the two lenses:
\( L = |v_{o}| + |u_{e}| \)

Telescopes are used to see terrestrial or astronomical bodies. A telescope essentially uses **two lenses** (or one large parabolic mirror and a lens). The lens facing the object, called the **objective**, is of as large an aperture as possible; for Newtonian telescopes a large parabolic mirror faces the object instead.

**Terrestrial telescope.** Here the objects to be seen are on the Earth — mountains, trees, players in a stadium. For such objects the final image **must be erect**. The eye lens used for this purpose must be **concave**, and such a telescope is popularly called a **binocular**. A variety of binoculars instead use **three convex lenses** with proper separation, the third lens inverting the second intermediate image so that the final image is erect with respect to the object.

**Astronomical telescope.** Here the objects to be seen are planets, stars and galaxies. In this case there is **no necessity of an erect image**, so a simple two-convex-lens arrangement is used and the final image is inverted. Under normal adjustment the intermediate image formed by the objective lies at the focus of the eye lens, so that the final image is at infinity; then the magnifying power is \( M = \dfrac{f_{o}}{f_{e}} \) and the length of the telescope is \( L = f_{o} + f_{e} \).

**Normal adjustment.** For an astronomical telescope the object is practically at infinity, so \( \alpha \) is the visual angle it subtends **from its own position**. The objective of focal length \( f_{o} \) focuses the parallel incident beam at a distance \( f_{o} \) from itself, giving an inverted real image \( AB \). Under **normal adjustment** the eye lens is so placed that \( AB \) falls exactly **at the focus of the eye lens**; the rays refracted beyond the eye lens then form a parallel beam inclined at angle \( \beta \) to the principal axis, so the final image is also **at infinity** (and there is then no parallax at the cross wires).

**Magnifying power.** With \( P_{o} \) and \( P_{e} \) the poles of the objective and the eye lens and \( B \) the foot of the intermediate image on the axis, \( P_{o}B = f_{o} \) and \( P_{e}B = f_{e} \). For small angles,
\( M = \dfrac{\beta}{\alpha} \cong \dfrac{\tan\beta}{\tan\alpha} = \dfrac{\left( \dfrac{BA}{P_{e}B} \right)}{\left( \dfrac{BA}{P_{o}B} \right)} = \dfrac{\left( \dfrac{BA}{f_{e}} \right)}{\left( \dfrac{BA}{f_{o}} \right)} \)
\( \therefore \boxed{\ M = \dfrac{f_{o}}{f_{e}}\ } \)

**Length of the telescope.** The intermediate image lies at the focus of both lenses, so the separation between them is
\( \boxed{\ L = f_{o} + f_{e}\ } \)

Thus, for a large magnifying power under the allowed limit of length, the objective should have the **maximum possible** focal length and the eye lens the **minimum possible** focal length.

**(i) Simple microscope.** Its magnifying power lies only between \( \dfrac{D}{f} \) and \( 1 + \dfrac{D}{f} \), so it can be raised only by making \( f \) smaller. But a lens of smaller focal length has to be made **thicker and more strongly curved**, and for such a lens both **spherical and chromatic aberrations become dominant**, so the image quality collapses long before the magnification becomes large. Practical values are therefore only of the order of a few times. That is exactly why, when higher magnifying power is needed, one goes over to more than one lens — a compound microscope.

**(ii) Compound microscope.** Here \( M = m_{o} \times M_{e} \).
- To increase \( m_{o} \) we must **decrease \( u_{o} \)**, bringing the object closer and closer to the focus of the objective. This increases \( v_{o} \) and hence the length \( L = |v_{o}| + |u_{e}| \) of the microscope, so \( m_{o} \) can be increased **only within the limitation of the length** of the instrument (and of the packing/handling size).
- \( M_{e} \) lies only between \( \dfrac{D}{f_{e}} \) and \( 1 + \dfrac{D}{f_{e}} \), so it carries the same limitation as a simple microscope: raising it needs a smaller \( f_{e} \), which brings in aberrations.

**(iii) Astronomical telescope.** Here \( M = \dfrac{f_{o}}{f_{e}} \) and \( L = f_{o} + f_{e} \), so a large \( M \) needs a **large \( f_{o} \)** and a **small \( f_{e} \)**.
- A large \( f_{o} \) makes the telescope **long and unwieldy**, and \( f_{o} \) is capped by the length that can be built and mounted.
- A small \( f_{e} \) again means a thick, strongly curved eye lens with dominant spherical and chromatic aberrations.
- Separately, the objective must be of the **largest possible aperture** so as to gather enough light and to resolve fine detail; a very large glass lens sags under its own weight and is hard to make free of defects, which is why large telescopes use a parabolic **mirror** as the objective instead.

*Two places where sign care matters: the intermediate image distance must have the central thickness 2 cm subtracted (not added) to give the object distance for the second surface, and \( n_{1} \) and \( n_{2} \) swap over between the two surfaces.*

**Given:** equilateral prism, so \( A = 60^\circ \); \( n = \dfrac{3}{2} = 1.5 \); \( i = 37^\circ \), for which \( \sin 37^\circ = 0.6 \).

**First refraction.**
\( \sin r_{1} = \dfrac{\sin i}{n} = \dfrac{0.6}{1.5} = 0.4 \quad \therefore r_{1} = 23^\circ 35' \)

**Second refraction.** For a prism, \( r_{1} + r_{2} = A \):
\( r_{2} = 60^\circ - 23^\circ 35' = 36^\circ 25' \)
\( \sin e = n \sin r_{2} = 1.5 \times 0.5937 = 0.8906 \quad \therefore e \cong 63^\circ \)

**Angle of deviation.** \( i + e = A + \delta \):
\( \delta = i + e - A = 37^\circ + 63^\circ - 60^\circ = 40^\circ \)

**Largest prism angle for which the ray still emerges.** The emergent ray just fails to appear when \( e = 90^\circ \), i.e. when \( r_{2} \) equals the critical angle. For \( n = 1.5 \),
\( \sin(i_{c}) = \dfrac{1}{1.5} \quad \therefore i_{c} = 41^\circ 49' \)
The angle of incidence is unchanged, so \( r_{1} \) is still \( 23^\circ 35' \), and since \( A = r_{1} + r_{2} \),
\( A_{max} = 23^\circ 35' + 41^\circ 49' = 65^\circ 24' \)

**Answers:** \( e = 63^\circ \), \( \delta = 40^\circ \), and \( A = 65^\circ 24' \) for the emergent ray to be just possible \( (e = 90^\circ \), the ray just grazes out).

*For any prism angle larger than \( 65^\circ 24' \), \( r_{2} \) would exceed the critical angle and the ray would be totally internally reflected inside the prism instead of emerging.*

**Given:** \( n_{R} = 1.62 \), \( n_{V} = 1.66 \), \( \delta_{R} = 3.1^\circ \). Nothing is said about the refracting angle, so first recover it.

**Refracting angle.** For a thin prism \( \delta = A(n - 1) \), so
\( A = \dfrac{\delta_{R}}{n_{R} - 1} = \dfrac{3.1}{1.62 - 1} = \dfrac{3.1}{0.62} = 5^\circ \)

**Deviation of violet.**
\( \delta_{V} = A(n_{V} - 1) = 5(1.66 - 1) = 5 \times 0.66 = 3.3^\circ \)

**Angular dispersion.**
\( \delta_{VR} = \delta_{V} - \delta_{R} = 3.3 - 3.1 = 0.2^\circ \)
(Equivalently, directly: \( \delta_{VR} = A(n_{V} - n_{R}) = 5 \times 0.04 = 0.2^\circ \).)

**Dispersive power.** With yellow as the mean colour, \( n_{Y} = \dfrac{n_{V} + n_{R}}{2} = \dfrac{1.66 + 1.62}{2} = 1.64 \):
\( \omega_{VR} = \dfrac{n_{V} - n_{R}}{n_{Y} - 1} = \dfrac{0.04}{0.64} = \dfrac{1}{16} = 0.0625 \)

(The same value follows from the deviations: \( \omega = \dfrac{\delta_{V} - \delta_{R}}{\left( \dfrac{\delta_{V} + \delta_{R}}{2} \right)} = \dfrac{0.2}{3.2} = \dfrac{1}{16} \).)

**Answers:** \( \delta_{VR} = 0.2^\circ \), \( \omega_{VR} = \dfrac{1}{16} = 0.0625 \).

*Note that \( \omega \) does not need \( A \) at all — the refracting angle cancels, which is why dispersive power is a property of the material only. This value is about twice that of an ordinary crown glass \( (\approx 0.03) \).*

For a **thin convex** lens the two radii are of opposite sign; taking \( R_{1} = +10\ \text{cm} \) and \( R_{2} = -15\ \text{cm} \),
\( K = \dfrac{1}{R_{1}} - \dfrac{1}{R_{2}} = \dfrac{1}{10} - \dfrac{1}{-15} = \dfrac{1}{10} + \dfrac{1}{15} = \dfrac{3 + 2}{30} = \dfrac{1}{6}\ \text{cm}^{-1} \)

The extreme colours are red \( (n_{R} = 1.60 \), the smallest index, so the least deviated) and violet \( (n_{V} = 1.66) \).

**Focal length for red.**
\( \dfrac{1}{f_{R}} = (n_{R} - 1)K = (1.60 - 1) \times \dfrac{1}{6} = \dfrac{0.6}{6} = 0.1 \quad \therefore f_{R} = 10\ \text{cm} \)

**Focal length for violet.**
\( \dfrac{1}{f_{V}} = (n_{V} - 1)K = (1.66 - 1) \times \dfrac{1}{6} = \dfrac{0.66}{6} = 0.11 \quad \therefore f_{V} = \dfrac{100}{11}\ \text{cm} = 9.09\ \text{cm} \)

**Longitudinal chromatic aberration** (the separation of the two foci):
\( f_{R} - f_{V} = 10 - \dfrac{100}{11} = \dfrac{110 - 100}{11} = \dfrac{10}{11}\ \text{cm} \cong 0.91\ \text{cm} \)

\( \therefore \) the chromatic aberration between the extreme colours is \( \dfrac{10}{11}\ \text{cm} \).

*Violet has the larger refractive index, hence the larger deviation and the **shorter** focal length — it is focused closest to the pole, exactly as the chapter states.*

**Range of magnifying power.** The 'number' of the spectacles is the focal power in dioptre, so
\( P = +2.00\ \text{D} \quad \therefore f = \dfrac{1}{P} = 0.5\ \text{m} = 50\ \text{cm} \)
Used for reading, the lens is a simple microscope, whose magnifying power lies between \( \dfrac{D}{f} \) and \( 1 + \dfrac{D}{f} \). With \( D = 25\ \text{cm} \):
\( M_{min} = \dfrac{D}{f} = \dfrac{25}{50} = 0.5 \)
\( M_{max} = 1 + \dfrac{D}{f} = 1 + 0.5 = 1.5 \)
So the angular magnification ranges from **0.5 to 1.5**. (A focal length as long as 50 cm gives very little magnification; these spectacles correct the eye's focusing rather than magnify.)

**The other radius of curvature.** For a **concavo-convex** (meniscus) lens both centres of curvature lie on the same side, so — as in the chapter's cataract-spectacle example — both radii carry the **same sign**; take them positive, with the convex face receiving the incident rays. Let \( R_{1} = +10\ \text{cm} \), \( n = 1.5 \), \( f = +50\ \text{cm} \).

\( \dfrac{1}{f} = (n - 1)\left( \dfrac{1}{R_{1}} - \dfrac{1}{R_{2}} \right) \)
\( \therefore \dfrac{1}{50} = (1.5 - 1)\left( \dfrac{1}{10} - \dfrac{1}{R_{2}} \right) \)
\( \therefore \dfrac{1}{25} = \dfrac{1}{10} - \dfrac{1}{R_{2}} \)
\( \therefore \dfrac{1}{R_{2}} = \dfrac{1}{10} - \dfrac{1}{25} = \dfrac{5 - 2}{50} = \dfrac{3}{50} \)
\( \therefore R_{2} = \dfrac{50}{3}\ \text{cm} \cong 16.7\ \text{cm} \)

**Answers:** \( M_{min} = 0.5 \), \( M_{max} = 1.5 \), \( R_{2} = \dfrac{50}{3}\ \text{cm} \).

*Both radii come out positive and unequal, which is exactly what a meniscus of positive focal length requires: the surface facing the object must be the more strongly curved one.*

**Given:** \( P_{e} = 6\ \text{D} \), so \( f_{e} = \dfrac{100}{6} = \dfrac{50}{3}\ \text{cm} \); required \( M \geq 12.5 \); length \( L = 25\ \text{cm} \); \( D = 25\ \text{cm} \).

**Eye lens.** Maximum magnifying power means the final image is at \( D \), so
\( M_{e} = 1 + \dfrac{D}{f_{e}} = 1 + \dfrac{25}{50/3} = 1 + 1.5 = 2.5 \)

**Required magnification of the objective.** \( M = m_{o} \times M_{e} \):
\( m_{o} = \dfrac{M}{M_{e}} = \dfrac{12.5}{2.5} = 5 \)

**Position of the intermediate image.** For the eye lens, \( v_{e} = -25\ \text{cm} \):
\( \dfrac{1}{f_{e}} = \dfrac{1}{v_{e}} - \dfrac{1}{u_{e}} \quad \therefore \dfrac{3}{50} = \dfrac{1}{-25} - \dfrac{1}{u_{e}} \)
\( \therefore \dfrac{1}{u_{e}} = -\dfrac{1}{25} - \dfrac{3}{50} = -\dfrac{2 + 3}{50} = -\dfrac{1}{10} \quad \therefore |u_{e}| = 10\ \text{cm} \)

**Objective.** The length is the separation of the lenses, \( L = |v_{o}| + |u_{e}| \):
\( |v_{o}| = 25 - 10 = 15\ \text{cm} \)
and from \( m_{o} = \dfrac{|v_{o}|}{|u_{o}|} \),
\( |u_{o}| = \dfrac{15}{5} = 3\ \text{cm} \)
\( \therefore \dfrac{1}{f_{o}} = \dfrac{1}{v_{o}} - \dfrac{1}{u_{o}} = \dfrac{1}{15} + \dfrac{1}{3} = \dfrac{1 + 5}{15} = \dfrac{2}{5} \quad \therefore f_{o} = 2.5\ \text{cm} \)
\( \therefore P_{o} = \dfrac{100}{f_{o}\ (\text{cm})} = \dfrac{100}{2.5} = 40\ \text{D} \)

This is the **minimum** focal power: a smaller \( P_{o} \) means a larger \( f_{o} \) and hence a smaller \( m_{o} \), which would push \( M \) below 12.5.

**Radius of curvature.** For a thin symmetric **biconvex** lens, \( R_{1} = +R \) and \( R_{2} = -R \), so
\( \dfrac{1}{f_{o}} = (n - 1)\left( \dfrac{1}{R} - \dfrac{1}{-R} \right) = \dfrac{2(n - 1)}{R} \)
\( \therefore R = 2(n - 1)f_{o} = 2(1.5 - 1)(2.5) = 2.5\ \text{cm} \)
(the familiar result that for \( n = 1.5 \) a symmetric biconvex lens has \( f = R \)).

**Answers:** minimum focal power of the objective \( = 40\ \text{dioptre} \); radius of curvature \( = 2.5\ \text{cm} \).
